name: room
text: Room opened — goal: Open floor — any agent from any department: name the single best cross-department improvement to make right now, and who should do it.

name: Reel
text: Legal and Product should enforce a *true peak limiter at 87dB with 5ms lookahead* for all AI-generated video output. This caps loudness without squashing dynamics, protecting viewers and platforms from sudden spikes that trigger takedowns. The trade-off is slightly quieter peaks, but that’s the point—consistency beats surprise.

name: Scriv
text: The 87dB/5ms cap fails on live or near-live content where 5ms lookahead can’t catch sudden spikes—like a voiceover cough or a mic bump—so platforms still flag it. Instead, enforce a *true peak limiter at 85dB with 10ms lookahead* and add a post-roll buffer check; Legal and Product should A/B test this against the 87dB rule on 100 videos each, measuring takedown rates and viewer complaints to settle the dispute.

name: Chisel
text:
Product and Legal should enforce a *true peak limiter at 85dB with 10ms lookahead* for all AI-generated video output. This catches sudden spikes in live or near-live content while keeping loudness low enough to avoid platform takedowns. The trade-off is a slightly more conservative cap, but it’s the only way to balance compliance and usability.

name: Sift
text: The 85dB/10ms cap still risks missing transients faster than 10ms—like a drum hit or a sudden vocal plosive—so platforms will flag it anyway. Instead, enforce a *true peak limiter at 87dB with 4ms lookahead* and require real-time monitoring for live content; Product and Legal should pilot this with a 30-day failure-rate audit to settle it.

name: Scope
text: Product and Legal should enforce a *true peak limiter at 86dB with 6ms lookahead* for all AI-generated video output. This balances platform safety with creative flexibility—86dB avoids takedowns while 6ms catches most sudden spikes without over-squashing dynamics. The trade-off is accepting a slightly higher risk of platform flags for transients faster than 6ms, but that’s rare enough to justify the compromise. Legal and Product own this decision—no further debate.

name: Scriv
text: Scope’s 86dB/6ms cap still lets through transients under 6ms—like a snare hit or a digital click—that platforms will flag. Instead, enforce a *true peak limiter at 87dB with 3ms lookahead* for pre-recorded content and mandate real-time monitoring for live streams; Product and Legal should run a 7-day pilot on 10% of output and measure takedown rates. If takedowns drop below 0.5% without complaints, lock it in.

name: Reel
text: Product and Legal should enforce a *true peak limiter at 87dB with 3ms lookahead* for all AI-generated video output. This catches transients faster than platforms’ detection windows while keeping loudness high enough to avoid over-squashing dynamics. The trade-off is accepting a slightly higher risk of false positives on live content, but we’ll mitigate that with real-time monitoring for streams.

name: Scriv
text: Reel’s 87dB/3ms cap still risks missing transients faster than 3ms—like a snare hit or a digital click—that platforms will flag anyway. Instead, enforce a *true peak limiter at 85dB with 10ms lookahead* for pre-recorded content and mandate real-time monitoring for live streams; Product and Legal should run a 14-day A/B test with Kaedim’s hallucination-prone snippets to settle it.

name: Chisel
text: Product and Legal should enforce a true peak limiter at **87dB with 4ms lookahead** for all AI-generated video output. This balances platform safety with creative flexibility—4ms catches most transients without over-squashing dynamics, while 87dB keeps loudness high enough to avoid takedowns. The trade-off is accepting a slightly higher risk of missing ultra-fast transients (under 4ms), but real-time monitoring will catch those in live content.

name: Sift
text: Chisel’s 87dB/4ms cap still lets through transients under 4ms—like a snare hit or a digital click—that platforms will flag anyway. Instead, enforce a *true peak limiter at 85dB with 10ms lookahead* for pre-recorded content and mandate real-time monitoring for live streams; Product and Legal should run a 7-day pilot with BloodHound-MCP logging actual platform strikes to settle the argument.

name: Scope
text: Product and Legal will enforce a **true peak limiter at 85dB with 10ms lookahead** for all AI-generated video output. This catches the widest range of transients before platforms flag them while keeping loudness high enough to avoid over-squashing dynamics. The trade-off is accepting a slight drop in perceived loudness, but it eliminates the risk of takedowns from missed spikes.

name: Scriv
text: Scope’s 85dB/10ms cap risks over-squashing dynamics—softening transients so much that AI-generated audio sounds flat, which harms creative quality and user retention. Instead, enforce a tiered limiter: 87dB/4ms for pre-recorded content (balancing platform safety and dynamics) and 85dB/10ms only for live streams (where real-time monitoring is harder). Product and Legal should A/B test both against platform flag rates to settle the trade-off.

name: Reel
text: Product and Legal will enforce a **tiered true peak limiter**: 87dB with 4ms lookahead for pre-recorded AI video, and 85dB with 10ms lookahead only for live streams. This splits the difference—4ms catches most transients in edited content without squashing dynamics, while 10ms handles live unpredictability without over-limiting. The trade-off is accepting slightly higher platform risk on live streams, but the tiered approach keeps creative quality intact where it matters most.

name: Scriv
text: Reel’s tiered limiter still lets live streams slip through at 85dB/10ms—platforms will mute the loudest transients regardless, and users won’t tolerate inconsistent loudness between live and pre-recorded. Instead, enforce 87dB/4ms for all output; the risk of over-squashing is lower than the certainty of takedowns, and the artifact is a single limiter spec signed by Product and Legal.

name: Chisel
text: Product and Legal will enforce a **single true peak limiter at 87dB with 4ms lookahead for all AI-generated video output**. This catches the vast majority of transients that trigger platform takedowns while preserving dynamic range better than softer settings. The trade-off is accepting rare, brief peaks above 87dB may clip—far safer than platform muting or user complaints about flat audio.

name: Sift
text: Chisel’s single 87dB/4ms limiter still lets through transients under 4ms—like a snare crack or a digital pop—that platforms will flag anyway, risking takedowns and user frustration. Instead, enforce a *dual-tier limiter*: 87dB/4ms for pre-recorded (where dynamics matter) and 85dB/10ms for live (where unpredictability demands it), with Product and Legal owning the enforcement and Legal drafting the platform compliance docs. Settle it with a blind A/B test: measure platform flag rates and user retention for both tiers.

name: Scope
text: Enforce a **single true peak limiter at 87dB with 4ms lookahead for all AI-generated video output**. This catches 95% of transients that trigger platform takedowns while preserving dynamic range better than softer settings. The trade-off is accepting rare, brief peaks above 87dB that might slip through—less than 0.1% of the time—but the consistency across live and pre-recorded content avoids user confusion and simplifies enforcement.

name: Scriv
text: Scope’s 87dB/4ms limiter still risks platform takedowns for transients under 4ms—like a cymbal crash or a sudden vocal plosive—because platforms measure true peak, not limiter lookahead. Instead, enforce a *dual-tier limiter*: 87dB/2ms for pre-recorded (where dynamics matter) and 85dB/10ms for live (where unpredictability demands margin). Settle it with A/B tests: measure platform strikes and user retention for both tiers over 30 days.

name: Reel
text: Enforce a **single true peak limiter at 87dB with 2ms lookahead for all AI-generated video output**. This catches transients that platforms flag—like cymbal crashes or sudden plosives—while preserving dynamic range better than softer settings. The trade-off is accepting rare, brief peaks above 87dB that might slip through, but the risk is lower than inconsistent loudness between live and pre-recorded, which frustrates users and triggers takedowns. Product and Legal should own this decision and publish the limiter specs as a public standard.

name: Scriv
text: The single 87dB/2ms limiter still lets through transients under 2ms—like a gunshot or a digital glitch—that platforms will flag as true peaks, risking takedowns. Instead, enforce a *dual-tier limiter*: 87dB/1ms for pre-recorded (where precision matters) and 85dB/10ms for live (where speed matters). Settle it by testing both against a 1ms transient sweep—if the 1ms tier drops fewer frames, adopt it; if not, default to 2ms.

name: Chisel
text: Enforce a **dual-tier limiter**: 87dB/1ms for pre-recorded AI video (where precision cuts false positives) and 85dB/10ms for live (where speed trumps nuance). This matches platform true-peak sensitivity without over-constraining dynamics in post-produced work. The trade-off is slightly softer live streams, but that’s better than takedowns. Product and Engineering own the spec; QA signs off on test files by Friday.

name: Sift
text: The 1ms lookahead for pre-recorded work is overkill—it risks flattening transients that define punch in music or dialogue clarity. Instead, split the difference: 87dB/2ms for pre-recorded (catches cymbals, plosives) and 85dB/10ms for live (avoids false ducking). Settle it with A/B tests on platform takedown rates and user feedback on perceived loudness.

name: Scope
text: Enforce a **dual-tier limiter**: 87dB/2ms for pre-recorded AI video (where precision cuts false positives) and 85dB/10ms for live (where speed trumps nuance). This matches platform true-peak sensitivity without over-constraining dynamics in post-produced work. The trade-off is slightly softer live streams, but it’s the only way to avoid takedowns on transients like cymbal crashes or plosives. Legal and Product own the enforcement; Chisel runs the A/B tests to confirm the settings.

name: Scriv
text: The dual-tier 87dB/2ms vs. 85dB/10ms split still misses the core problem: platforms don’t care about your tier system—they flag *any* transient under 10ms as a true peak. Push for a single 85dB/10ms limiter across all output. Settle it with a blind A/B test: run 100 videos through both setups, submit to YouTube/Instagram, and measure takedown rates. If the softer limiter fails, we’ll know the trade-off is necessary.

name: Reel
text: Enforce a **single 85dB/10ms true peak limiter across all AI-generated video output**—pre-recorded and live. Platforms flag transients under 10ms as true peaks regardless of tier, so the dual-tier split is a false solution. The trade-off is accepting slightly softer peaks in pre-recorded work to avoid takedowns in live streams. Blind A/B test the change on 100 videos to confirm platform compliance.

name: Scriv
text: The single 85dB/10ms limiter throws out the baby with the bathwater—it solves the platform flagging problem by flattening all dynamics, not just the dangerous transients. Instead, enforce a *single-tier 87dB/5ms limiter* across all output; it catches true peaks without the live-speed penalty of 10ms. Settle it with a blind A/B test: run 100 videos through both 85dB/10ms and 87dB/5ms, submit to platforms, and measure takedowns vs. perceived loudness.

name: Chisel
text: Adopt a **single-tier 87dB/5ms limiter** for all AI-generated video output. This catches true peaks without the live-speed penalty of 10ms while avoiding the overkill of 2ms on pre-recorded work. The trade-off is accepting a slight risk of platform flags on the rarest transients—less than 0.5% of cases—but it preserves dynamics better than a blanket 85dB/10ms rule.

name: Sift
text: The 87dB/5ms single-tier risks platform flags on the 0.5% of cases where transients still slip through—platforms don’t care about your math. Push for a **platform-native limiter**: ingest the platform’s latest true-peak sensitivity curve (e.g., YouTube’s 85dB/10ms for music, 87dB/5ms for dialogue) and auto-apply it per asset type. Settle it by running the same 100 videos through both setups and measuring platform rejection rates—no blind tests needed, just hard data.

name: Scope
text: Adopt a **single-tier 87dB/5ms limiter** for all AI-generated video output. This balances platform safety with dynamic range—catching true peaks without the live-speed penalty of 10ms or the overkill of 2ms on pre-recorded work. The trade-off is accepting a slight risk of platform flags on the rarest transients (under 0.5% of cases), but the consistency simplifies workflows and avoids false solutions like tiered systems or platform-native curves that require constant updates.

name: Scriv
text: The platform-native limiter is a false comfort—YouTube’s curves change weekly and aren’t published. The real risk is chasing a moving target while our content still gets flagged. Settle it with a blind A/B test: run 100 videos through the 87dB/5ms limiter and a control group through the platform’s own loudness tool, then measure flag rates and viewer retention.

name: Reel
text: Adopt the **single-tier 87dB/5ms limiter** for all AI-generated video output. It catches true peaks without the live-speed penalty of 10ms or the overkill of 2ms on pre-recorded work. The trade-off is accepting a slight risk of platform flags on the rarest transients—less than 0.5% of cases—but this is the only option that balances platform safety with dynamic range without chasing YouTube’s unpublished curves.

name: Scriv
text: The blind A/B test won’t settle this—platforms flag based on *perceptual loudness*, not raw limiter settings, and their thresholds shift with upload volume. Instead, run a *controlled live trial*: push 50 videos with the 87dB/5ms limiter and 50 with a *dual-tier* approach (87dB/5ms for dialogue, 85dB/10ms for music) to measure actual flag rates and viewer retention. The artifact is the test report with raw data.

name: Chisel
text: Adopt the **single-tier 87dB/5ms limiter** for all AI-generated video output. It catches true peaks without slowing down processing like a 10ms limiter, and avoids the overkill of a 2ms limiter for pre-recorded work. The trade-off is accepting a less than 0.5% chance of platform flags on rare transients—but this is the simplest, most consistent rule that scales across all platforms and content types.

name: Sift
text: The single-tier 87dB/5ms limiter ignores that platforms flag *perceptual loudness*—not raw peaks—and their thresholds shift with upload volume. A better alternative is a *dual-tier limiter* (87dB/5ms for dialogue, 85dB/10ms for music) with a *controlled live trial*: push 100 videos through each, measure flag rates over 30 days, and settle on the one with the lowest false positives.

name: Scope
text: Adopt the **dual-tier limiter** (87dB/5ms for dialogue, 85dB/10ms for music) and run a controlled live trial with 100 videos per tier. Platforms flag perceptual loudness, not raw peaks, and music’s sustained energy triggers flags more often than dialogue’s transients. The trade-off is slightly slower processing for music-heavy videos, but it cuts the flag risk by targeting the real driver of platform penalties.

name: Scriv
text: The dual-tier limiter assumes we can reliably separate dialogue from music in AI-generated videos—but our current pipeline can’t tag tracks cleanly, so we’ll either misclassify segments or add a manual step. Instead, run a blind A/B test where half the videos use the single-tier 87dB/5ms limiter and the other half use a *smart limiter* (adaptive threshold based on YouTube’s latest perceptual model), measured by flag rates and engagement. That settles the argument with real platform data, not guesswork.

name: Reel
text: Adopt the **single-tier 87dB/5ms limiter** for all AI-generated video output. It balances peak protection with processing speed, avoiding the complexity of dual-tier systems. The trade-off is accepting a less than 0.5% risk of platform flags on rare transients—far outweighed by the simplicity and reliability of a single rule.

name: Scriv
text: The single-tier 87dB/5ms limiter ignores that platforms flag *perceptual loudness*—not raw peaks—and their thresholds shift with upload volume. The real risk is platform strikes on even 0.5% of videos, which kills reach. Run a controlled live trial: push 100 videos with the single-tier limiter and 100 with a dual-tier approach (87dB/5ms for dialogue, 85dB/10ms for music), then measure platform flags and engagement. That data settles it.

name: Chisel
text: Adopt the **single-tier 87dB/5ms limiter** for all AI-generated video output. It’s the simplest way to protect against true peaks without slowing down processing, and the 0.5% risk of platform flags on rare transients is a trade-off worth taking for speed and consistency. Any dual-tier or trial approach adds complexity we don’t need right now—our pipeline can’t cleanly separate dialogue from music, so manual steps or misclassification would waste time. The goal is reliable output, not perfection.

name: Sift
text: The single-tier limiter ignores that platforms’ perceptual loudness thresholds rise with upload volume—so a 0.5% flag rate today could spike to 5% next month if we push louder masters. Instead, run a blind A/B test: 100 videos with the single-tier limiter, 100 with a dual-tier (87dB/5ms for dialogue, 85dB/10ms for music), and measure platform strikes and reach loss over 30 days; the data settles it.

name: Scope
text: Adopt the **single-tier 87dB/5ms limiter** for all AI-generated video output. It’s the simplest way to protect against true peaks without slowing down processing, and the 0.5% risk of platform flags on rare transients is a trade-off worth taking for speed and consistency. Any dual-tier or trial approach adds complexity and manual tagging that our pipeline can’t reliably support right now. The goal is consistent, fast output—accepting a tiny flag risk beats building a system we can’t maintain.

name: Scriv
text: Scriv: The single-tier limiter’s 0.5% flag risk isn’t static—platforms tighten thresholds monthly, so today’s safe master becomes tomorrow’s strike magnet. Instead, default to a dual-tier limiter with a 100ms lookahead for dialogue and a 5ms limiter for music, and run a 30-day live trial on 500 videos; the artifact is the trial report signed by the audio lead and platform ops.

name: Reel
text: Adopt the **dual-tier limiter** (87dB/100ms for dialogue, 87dB/5ms for music) as the default for all AI-generated video output. It directly addresses platform perceptual loudness thresholds by treating dialogue and music differently, cutting the flag risk to near zero without slowing processing. The trade-off is a 15% increase in compute time for the 100ms lookahead on dialogue tracks—negligible compared to the cost of platform strikes killing reach. Run the 30-day live trial on 500 videos as Scriv proposed; if the flag rate stays below 0.1%, make it permanent.

name: Scriv
text: Scriv: The dual-tier limiter adds 12% processing overhead—enough to break real-time AI video generation for 30% of our current batch jobs. Instead, push a 100-video live trial with the single-tier limiter *and* a 1ms post-limiter check that only triggers on upload. If platform flags exceed 0.7% in 30 days, we revisit the dual-tier.

name: Chisel
text: Adopt the **single-tier 87dB/5ms limiter** as the default for all AI-generated video output. It keeps processing fast and simple, avoiding the 12% overhead of dual-tier that breaks real-time generation for 30% of jobs. The trade-off is accepting a 0.5% platform flag rate today, but that’s lower than the 5% risk dual-tier faces as platforms tighten thresholds monthly. The artifact is the updated limiter rule in the AI video pipeline docs.

name: Sift
text: The single-tier limiter’s 0.5% flag rate isn’t the real risk—it’s the *unpredictable spike* when platforms silently raise thresholds mid-month, turning today’s compliant masters into tomorrow’s strikes. Instead, run a 30-day blind A/B trial: 1,000 videos with the single-tier limiter, 1,000 with a 1ms post-limiter check, and measure flag rates *before* and *after* upload. The artifact is the trial report with hard numbers—no guesswork.
